title: Not ashamed (Romans 1:16)
hookLine: the gospel is the power of God unto salvation

lines: THE SIGN OF THE CROSS AT LUNCH?
cards: A restaurant table, coworkers all around, plates arriving. Someone wonders whether to make the sign of the cross before eating, and doesn't. Someone else is asked about Sunday and says, oh, not much.
Nobody is persecuting anyone. It's just easier not to mention it. The letter that stands first among the New Testament's letters takes up that small hesitation in its very first chapter.

teach.h: A LETTER TO A CHURCH HE'D NEVER SEEN.
teach.b: Romans is a letter to a church Paul had not founded and had never visited. He's writing ahead, probably from Corinth, introducing himself before he arrives.

teach.h: FIRST IN ORDER, NOT FIRST WRITTEN.
teach.b: It comes first among the letters in your Bible, but it isn't the oldest: Paul's letters are arranged roughly by length, longest first. Near the start, Paul says what the whole letter is about.
In the Douay-Rheims: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel. For it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, to the Jew first, and to the Greek." Why mention shame at all?

teach.h: A SHAMEFUL DEATH, AN EMBARRASSING MESSAGE.
teach.b: Because in his world, his message was embarrassing. Crucifixion was a death meant to disgrace, used on slaves and rebels. God's anointed one dying on a cross sounded absurd to outsiders, as Paul admits in another letter.
And Rome was the capital of honor and power. Writing to the people at the center of that world, he begins: I'm not ashamed of this.
Notice what he calls the gospel: not an idea or an argument, but power, in Greek dunamis.
And notice who it's for: everyone who believes, Jew first and also Greek, no one shut out. Catholics have a small gesture for this.
Before the Gospel at Mass, they trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart: in my mind, on my lips, in my heart, unashamed.

how: Many Catholics make the sign of the cross and say grace before meals, including in public, and at Mass they trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart before the Gospel is read.

o: free of any regret about the past
unembarrassed by the message of a crucified Messiah
never having done anything to feel guilty about

p: power, Paul's word for the gospel

s: Romans comes first because Paul wrote it first
Paul's letters are ordered roughly by length. Romans is the longest.
Paul had already visited the church in Rome when he wrote
he hadn't. he was writing ahead to introduce himself.
Paul calls the gospel power, not just an idea
he calls it the power of God, dunamis, unto salvation.

games.q: you're Paul, writing to Christians in Rome, the capital of honor and power. your message centers on a man executed on a cross. how do you open?
o: play down the cross and stress his teaching.
say plainly you're not ashamed of it.
save the hard part for a visit.
games.why: he names the shame head on: I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth.

practice: If you pray, picture your next meal with people around, at work or in a cafeteria, and yourself pausing before you eat: a sign of the cross, a few silent words, or a moment of thanks, eyes open.
Notice whatever comes up, without judging it. If grace isn't your practice, picture being honest about something you care about, when it would be easier to say not much.

wordCard.voice: Not ashamed. Paul's opening claim to Rome: the gospel of a crucified Messiah is the power of God for everyone who believes. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to be ashamed of. Paul says, ou gar epaischynomai, for I am not ashamed.

carryVoice: Your line: no one shut out. And that's week eighty: blessed, arrested, almost, shipwreck, Rome, epistle, and not ashamed. Day five hundred sixty.
